This filter is a probabilistic machine learning (ML) based solution that is context-dependent\\nand detects sensitive information based on the context within input prompts or model responses. If sensitive information is detected in\\n the prompt or response, the guardrail blocks all the content and returns a\\n message that you configure.\\n* **Mask** \u2014 Sensitive information filter\\n policies can anonymize or redact information from model requests or responses.\\n For example, guardrails mask PIIs while generating summaries of conversations\\n between users and customer service agents. For more\\n information, see Remove PII from conversations by using sensitive information filters.\\n* **Detect** \u2013 Take no action but return what the\\n guardrail detects in the trace response. Use this option, known as\\n *detect mode*, to help evaluate whether your guardrail is\\n working the way that you expect\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/guardrails-harmful-content-handling-options.html\"},{\"rank_order\":3,\"title\":\"Create your guardrail\",\"context\":\"# Create your guardrail\\n\\nAmazon Bedrock Guardrails offers filters that you can configure to\\nhelp avoid undesirable and harmful content and remove or mask sensitive information for\\nprivacy protection.\\n\\nYou can configure the following filters with Amazon Bedrock Guardrails:\\n\\n* **Content filters** \u2014 This filter helps you detect and filter harmful\\n text or image content in input prompts or model responses (excluding reasoning content). Filtering is done based\\n on detection of certain predefined harmful content categories: Hate, Insults,\\n Sexual, Violence, Misconduct and Prompt Attack. You can configure the filter\\n strength for each of these categories based on your use cases. With Standard tier, detection of undesirable content is extended to protect against harmful content within code elements including\\n comments, variable and function names, and string literals.\\n* **Prompt attacks** \u2014 Offered as a category within content filters, this filter can help you detect and\\n filter prompt attacks including jailbreaks, prompt injections, and prompt leakages (Standard tier only). This capability helps you detect prompts that are intended\\n to bypass content moderation, override instructions, or generate harmful content.\\n* **Denied topics** \u2014 You can define a set of\\n topics to avoid within your generative AI application. For example, a banking\\n assistant application can be designed to help avoid topics related to illegal\\n investment advice. With Standard tier,\\n content filters extend to code domains.\\n* **Word filters** \u2014 You can define a set of\\n custom words or phrases (exact match) that you want to detect and block in the\\n interaction between your users and generative AI applications. For example, you can\\n detect and block profanity (using a ready-to-use option) as well as specific custom words such as competitor\\n names, or other offensive words.\\n* **Sensitive information filters** \u2014 Can help\\n you detect sensitive content such as Personally Identifiable Information (PII) in\\n standard formats or custom regex entities in user inputs and FM responses. This filter is a probabilistic maching learning (ML)\\n based solution that is context dependent. It detects sensitive information based on the context within input prompts or model responses. Based on\\n your use case, you can block or mask inputs and responses containing sensitive information. For example, you can redact users' personal information while\\n generating summaries from customer and agent conversation transcripts.\\n* **Contextual grounding checks** \u2014 Can\\n\\n*[truncated \u2014 additional content omitted]*\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/guardrails-components.html\"},{\"rank_order\":4,\"title\":\"Amazon Bedrock\",\"context\":\"##### 4. Sensitive Information Filters\\n\\nBlock or mask PII and sensitive data (SSN, date of birth, address, etc.). Detection is probabilistic. Custom regex patterns supported for organization-specific PII\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/gen-ai-inference-architecture-and-best-practices-on-aws/amazon-bedrock.html\"},{\"rank_order\":5,\"title\":\"How do I optimize prompts to achieve deterministic responses on Amazon Bedrock?\",\"context\":\"### Set up guardrails\\n\\nTo control the responses from the FMs, set up guardrails for Amazon Bedrock. You can consistently apply the guardrails across multiple FMs. Use guardrails to [block certain topics](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/guardrails-components.html#guardrails-topic-policies), [filter out harmful or unpredictable content](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/guardrails-components.html#guardrails-content-filters), remove undesirable words, and hide sensitive information. For more information, see [Guardrails for Amazon Bedrock](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/guardrails.html).\\n\\nYou can also customize blocked messages and\u00a0[use the built-in test window to test your guardrail configurations](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/guardrails-test.html). To get controlled and predictable outputs, connect guardrails directly with the FMs when you generate responses\",\"url\":\"https://repost.aws/knowledge-center/bedrock-prompts-deterministic-responses\"}]}}"}]}], "label": "Running Verify Aws Claim"}

{"id": "91097c71-fa9c-47ab-929f-76e6208dc845", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "I'm assuming this is an Amazon Bedrock guardrail's sensitive information filter. The docs I checked don't describe an allowlist or exception list for built-in PII types. So the fix is to narrow what the filter detects, not to exempt ticket IDs.

**1. Find which entity type is matching.**
- In mask mode the guardrail replaces the text with the entity type, such as `{NAME}` or `{USERNAME}`. Look at what `ABC-1234` becomes.
- You can also set the action to **Detect** on that filter, or call ApplyGuardrail, and read the trace. It lists the matched entity type and the text it matched.

**2. Remove or change that entity type.**
- The filter is ML-based and context-dependent, so a short alphanumeric code can be read as an ID, username, account number or similar.
- If you don't need that built-in type, remove it from the guardrail's PII list.
- If you do need it, set its action to **Detect** only (no masking) for input, output, or both, depending on where the false positives happen.

**3. Cover the real PII with custom regex instead.**
- Custom regex entities use exact pattern matching, so they won't catch `ABC-1234`.
- For example, if the built-in type was only there for one specific ID format, replace it with a regex for that format.

**4. Test before rolling out.** Run sample prompts containing ticket IDs in the guardrail test window, or through ApplyGuardrail, to confirm they pass and real PII is still caught.

**Caveats**
- Because the filter is probabilistic, a built-in type that stays enabled can still occasionally flag ID-like strings. Custom regex is the more deterministic option.
- The filter only evaluates text. It doesn't cover tool-call arguments, tool results or tool definitions.

Which entity tag shows up when `ABC-1234` is masked? Tell me, and I can suggest whether to drop that type or replace it with a regex. If you give me the guardrail ID and region, I can also look at its current configuration.", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
